prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map captures the continuous 3D geometry of the reception area, showing a wooden counter in the immediate foreground (0.3 to 1.2 m away) that recedes alongside a long corridor on the right extending over 5 m into the dark background. Across frames 1 to 4, a person with a handbag stands on the far left at 0.4 to 0.7 m (partially cropped out of view in frames 2 to 4) while a receptionist sits behind the counter about 1.2 to 1.5 m in front of the camera wearer and roughly 1.0 to 1.2 m to the right of the left person, facing forward toward the counter and camera wearer behind a monitor, telephone, and receipt printer that partially occlude their lower torso. In frames 2 to 4, a hand enters the lower-right foreground at 0.4 to 0.6 m, and as the camera wearer turns rightward in frame 5, the receptionist shifts to the far left edge while the person in the red shirt on the right is revealed standing 0.6 to 0.9 m away (about 1.5 m from the receptionist), facing and looking toward the camera wearer with their right hand resting on the counter edge. Near-white intensities show that the front edge of the counter, the handbag on the left, and the right-hand person's extended hand are within arm's reach of the camera wearer (under 0.8 m), whereas the monitor, printer, and clipboard sit within the receptionist's reach. This map makes the smooth distance gradient along the counter surface and corridor wall much clearer than the RGB image alone, though it is unreliable on thin or transparent objects like the spray bottle on the counter (which blurs into the background depth) and flattens fine facial and hand contours into uniform silhouettes.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates discrete foreground entities against the unlabelled counter and corridor, localizing the person and handbag on the far left (0.4 to 0.7 m away), the seated receptionist in the center-left (1.2 to 1.5 m away, facing the camera wearer), countertop items in front of the receptionist, and the person on the right (0.5 to 0.9 m away, about 1.5 m from the receptionist) who faces and looks toward the camera wearer in frame 5. It shows the receptionist positioned behind and slightly above the counter equipment (labelled as 'laptop') and to the left of the clipboard (labelled as 'book'), with the lower half of the receptionist occluded by the counter and equipment, while the left-hand person is partially out of view at the left frame boundary in frames 1, 3, and 4 and fully out of view in frames 2 and 5. Across the five frames, the masks track the camera wearer's pan to the right, capturing the right-side person initially as just a cropped hand and arm in the lower-right corner of frames 2 and 3 (within 0.6 m, arm's reach of the camera wearer) before revealing their full upper body in frame 5 with a card (labelled as 'remote') within both their own and the camera wearer's arm's reach. While the masks clearly separate overlapping silhouettes such as the receptionist's torso behind the monitor and the left person's body against the handbag better than raw RGB textures, the map is unreliable in its semantic labels and temporal consistency. Specifically, it misclassifies the desktop monitor and telephone as 'laptop', the clipboard as 'book', the card as 'remote', the handbag in frame 4 as part of a 'person', the wooden lattice screen above the receptionist in frame 4 as a 'tv', and the spray bottle in frame 5 as a 'person' and 'book', while completely missing the receptionist in frame 4.
descriptions.pose: The body and hand skeleton map tracks sparse 2D joint keypoints and limb orientations in the reception scene, detecting the receptionist's left hand on the counter in frame 1 (about 1.2 m away), the receptionist's upper-body skeleton behind the counter in frames 2 and 3 (1.2 to 1.5 m away), a nearby hand in the lower-right corner of frame 2 (about 0.5 m away), and the right-side person's upper body, facial keypoints, and right hand in frame 5 (0.6 to 0.9 m away). In frames 2 and 3, the receptionist's shoulder and arm vectors angle forward and downward onto the counter surface within their arm's reach, with their lower body occluded by the counter and monitor. As the camera wearer turns right by frame 5, the receptionist passes out of the tracked area on the left while the person on the right stands 0.6 to 0.9 m in front of the camera wearer (roughly 1.5 m from the receptionist's position), with symmetric shoulder keypoints and centered facial keypoints confirming their torso and head face directly toward the camera wearer while their right arm extends forward and downward to place their magenta-mapped hand on the counter within arm's reach of both themselves and the camera wearer. The explicit finger and limb segments make exact hand articulation and shoulder orientation easier to read at a glance than in the motion-blurred RGB frames. However, the map is highly unreliable in coverage and stability: it completely misses the person on the far left across all frames, drops the receptionist's skeleton entirely in frames 1, 4, and 5, misses the lower-right hand in frames 3 and 4, and produces distorted, collapsed shoulder-and-head geometry for the receptionist in frames 2 and 3.
